# Ep 2 Script — "What to Automate FIRST in Your Small Business (7 Tasks)"

**OWNS THE QUESTION:** What should a small business automate first?
**TARGET KEYWORD:** what to automate first small business

### [0:00–0:15] COLD-OPEN HOOK
**NARRATION:** "Most small business owners automate the wrong thing first. They pick the task
that's annoying instead of the task that pays. There's a simple rule that tells you exactly
where to start — and in the next few minutes I'll give you the rule, then rank the seven tasks
so you know your number one before this video ends."
**[VISUAL]:** Owner staring at a whiteboard covered in messy arrows → hard cut to a single clean
line labeled "START HERE." On-screen text: **"Automate the RIGHT thing first."**

### [0:15–0:40] GEO ANSWER BLOCK ← citation target
**NARRATION:** "Here's the direct answer. A small business should automate its high-frequency,
low-judgment tasks first — the work you repeat many times a day that doesn't need your personal
judgment to get right. I call it the Frequency-Judgment Rule: the more often a task happens, and
the less thinking it takes, the sooner you should hand it to AI. By that rule, the first task
for most businesses is answering repetitive customer questions."
**[VISUAL]:** A 2x2 grid appears and stays. Vertical axis "How often." Horizontal axis "How much
judgment." Top-left box glows: **"HIGH frequency + LOW judgment = automate FIRST."** (This
on-screen text = the citable answer.)

### [0:40–1:05] VALUE PROMISE + OPEN LOOP
**NARRATION:** "By the end you'll have your first automation picked — not a vague list, one task.
I'll rank all seven from fastest payback to slowest, and I'll give you a two-word test that tells
you if a task pays back in weeks or months. Stick around for number seven — it feels urgent, but
it's the one you should almost always do last, and I'll show you why."
**[VISUAL]:** Seven numbered chips slide in; chip 7 flashes a small "wait" icon.

### [1:05–1:35] WHY THE RULE WORKS (authority + freshness)
**NARRATION:** "Quick reason this rule holds up. As of 2026, seventy-seven percent of small
businesses already use at least one AI tool, and two-thirds save between five hundred and two
thousand dollars a month. But the ones who feel it fastest didn't automate the hardest thing —
they automated the most repeated thing. Frequency is the multiplier. Save two minutes on a task
you do four times a day and you just bought back real hours by Friday."
**[VISUAL]:** Three stat cards animate in: **77% · $500–$2,000/mo · +40% productivity.** Small
source line.
**[PATTERN INTERRUPT]:** Punchy zoom on the word **"Frequency is the multiplier."**
> The best first automation isn't your hardest task — it's your most repeated one.

### [1:35–3:00] TASKS 1–2 — THE INSTANT WINS (high frequency, low judgment)
**NARRATION:** "So let's rank them. Numbers one and two are your instant wins — high frequency,
low judgment, fastest payback. Number one: answering FAQs. The same handful of questions,
answered for you, day and night, in seconds. Number two: data entry — copying names, orders, and
details between your inbox, your spreadsheet, and your tools. It's pure repetition with almost no
judgment, which is exactly what software is best at. These two usually pay for themselves inside
a week."
**[VISUAL]:** Split screen. Left: a chatbot firing back FAQ answers. Right: fields
auto-filling from an email into a spreadsheet. Rank badges "#1" and "#2."
**[TAKEAWAY on screen]:** "#1 FAQs · #2 Data entry — high frequency, low judgment, pay back in
days."
**[PATTERN INTERRUPT]:** Counter ticks "1 email → 0 typing."

### [3:00–4:20] TASKS 3–4 — THE RELIABLE MIDDLE (steady frequency, still low judgment)
**NARRATION:** "Numbers three and four still score high on the rule, just slightly less often.
Number three: appointment reminders — the texts and emails that cut no-shows, sent automatically
before every booking. Number four: invoice reminders — a polite nudge that fires when a payment's
late so you stop chasing money by hand. Both are low judgment. Both happen on a schedule. And
number four literally puts cash back in your account, which is why it ranks above the fancier
stuff."
**[VISUAL]:** A calendar sends a reminder → "no-show rate down." Then an invoice flips from
"overdue" to "reminder sent."
**[TAKEAWAY]:** "#3 Appointment reminders · #4 Invoice reminders — set once, they run on
schedule."
> A task that runs on a schedule is begging to be automated — you're just the alarm clock.

**NARRATION:** "So four tasks in, and notice the pattern — we're not ranking by how impressive
the AI is, we're ranking by how often the task repeats. That's the whole game. Three more to go,
including the one that makes money and the one you should hold off on. Real quick — this is a

Episode 3, and I answer it straight. Subscribe so it lands in your feed."

### [5:00–6:20] TASKS 5–6 — HIGHER JUDGMENT, HIGHER UPSIDE
**NARRATION:** "Numbers five and six need a little more judgment, so they rank lower — but the
upside climbs. Number five: lead first-reply. When someone new reaches out, AI sends a fast,
personal first response in seconds and hands you the warm ones. Speed wins deals, so this saves
time and makes money. Number six: pulling reports — AI gathers your sales and cash numbers and
tells you what changed, in plain English, instead of you building a spreadsheet on Sunday night.
Great payback, just a notch more setup and oversight than the first four."
**[VISUAL]:** Lead funnel: new lead → instant reply → "you take the warm ones." Then a messy
spreadsheet collapses into a three-line summary.
**[TAKEAWAY]:** "#5 Lead first-reply · #6 Report pulling — more judgment, bigger upside."
**[PATTERN INTERRUPT]:** Text slam: **"Speed is the sale."**
> The faster a lead hears back, the more likely they buy — even a machine's reply beats your
> silence.

### [6:20–7:25] TASK 7 — THE ONE TO DO LAST (the payoff)
**NARRATION:** "And number seven, the sleeper — social media scheduling. It feels urgent because
it's public and you see everyone else doing it. But posting is higher judgment than it looks —
tone, timing, what actually fits your brand — and it rarely pays back as fast as the boring stuff.
So automate it, sure, just not first. Do it once your instant wins are already buying back hours.
That's the trap the rule saves you from: chasing the visible task instead of the valuable one."
**[VISUAL]:** A flashy "POST NOW" button dimming while "#1 FAQs" and "#2 Data entry" glow
brighter beside it. Rank badge "#7" with a small clock.
**[PAYOFF of open loop]:** callback to "the one you should do last" from the intro.

### [7:25–8:05] THE WEEKS-VS-MONTHS TEST
**NARRATION:** "Before you pick, here's the two-word test I promised: **frequency and judgment**.
Ask two questions. How many times a day does this happen? And how much of my personal judgment
does it really need? Many times a day plus little judgment equals payback in weeks — start there.
A few times a month plus lots of judgment equals payback in months — that one waits. Run every
task on your list through those two questions and the order sorts itself out."
**[VISUAL]:** Two-question card: **"1. How often? 2. How much judgment?"** → arrow to
**"Weeks vs Months."**

### [8:05–8:45] CLOSE — PAYOFF + CTA + NEXT EPISODE
**NARRATION:** "So there's your ranking: FAQs, data entry, appointment reminders, invoice
reminders, lead first-reply, report pulling, and last, social scheduling — ordered by the
Frequency-Judgment Rule. Don't start all seven. Pick the one thing you do most often that needs
you least, and automate just that this week. Then the big question is what this means for your
team — will AI replace your employees? That's Episode 3. Watch it next, and I'll see you there."
